To recollect means to remember something, especially by making a conscious, deliberate effort to bring it back to mind from your memory.

The key idea here is effort. When you recollect something, you are not passively receiving a memory that floats up on its own — you are actively reaching back into your mind and searching for it. Think of your memory as a vast storage room. To recollect is to walk into that room and deliberately look for something.
The Feeling of Effort Inside the Word

This is the most important thing to understand about "recollect."

When you remember something, it can happen effortlessly — a smell might suddenly make you remember your grandmother's kitchen. No searching required.

But when you recollect something, there is usually a sense that you are trying — sometimes straining — to retrieve a memory that is not immediately clear or obvious. The memory might be distant, faint, or buried under time. You pause, think, and pull it back.

This is why "recollect" is very often used:

  • when someone is unsure whether they can remember something
  • when someone is reflecting on the past carefully
  • when the memory in question is old or not easily accessible

"I'm trying to recollect where I've seen her before."

Here, the speaker is clearly making a mental effort — it's not an instant memory.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Remember, recall, and recollect are close in meaning, but they carry slightly different shades.

  • Remember is the most general and everyday word. It covers both effortless and effortful memories. You can use it in almost any situation.
  • Recall is similar to recollect — it also suggests deliberate retrieval. However, "recall" often feels more sharp and precise, like pulling up specific facts or details quickly. It can also feel slightly more formal.
  • Recollect carries the most sense of slow, thoughtful, reflective remembering. It is the word you would use when you are sitting quietly and carefully searching your memory, especially for past events or experiences. It has a slightly old-fashioned, literary quality compared to "recall."

Think of it this way:

  • "I can't remember his name." — plain, everyday, neutral
  • "I can't recall his name." — slightly more deliberate, formal
  • "I can't quite recollect his name." — reflective, searching, slightly more formal or literary
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar)

Recollect is a transitive verb, meaning it typically takes an object — something that is being remembered. Here are the most common sentence patterns:

1. Recollect + noun (a thing/person/event)

"She could not recollect the exact date."
"I recollect that summer very well."

2. Recollect + that + clause

"I recollect that he was quite nervous during the meeting."
"She recollected that the door had been left open."

3. Recollect + -ing (a past action)

"I don't recollect seeing him at the party."
"He recollected hearing a strange noise that night."

4. Recollect + question word (where/when/who/what/how)

"Can you recollect where you put your passport?"
"I can't recollect when we first met."

Recollect sits on the more formal and literary end of the spectrum. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • literary fiction and older novels
  • formal or careful speech
  • courtroom or official testimony ("As far as I can recollect...")
  • thoughtful essays or memoirs

In everyday casual conversation, most people would simply say "remember" instead. If someone said "I don't recollect" in a casual chat with a friend, it might sound a little stiff or old-fashioned — though perfectly correct.

These examples will show you the word in action across different situations:

"The old man sat quietly, trying to recollect the name of the street where he had grown up."

— A slow, reflective effort to retrieve an old memory.

"I vaguely recollect meeting her at a conference, but I'm not entirely sure."

— The memory is uncertain and incomplete — classic territory for "recollect."

"Do you recollect what time the train was supposed to arrive?"

— A question asking someone to make an effort to remember.

"She recollected, with a sharp pang, the last conversation she had with her father."

— Bringing a meaningful past memory deliberately to mind.

"As far as I can recollect, no one mentioned anything about a change in plans."

— A very common formal phrase, signaling that the speaker is offering their best memory, not absolute certainty.

"He could not recollect ever having made such a promise."

— Searching the memory and finding nothing — a very natural use.

These are ready-made phrases you will frequently see "recollect" appear in:

  • "as far as I can recollect" — meaning: to the best of my memory
  • "I don't recollect" — meaning: I don't remember (often implying some searching)
  • "if I recollect correctly" — meaning: if my memory is right
  • "I vaguely recollect" — a partial, uncertain memory
  • "try to recollect" — an explicit effort to remember

Be careful not to confuse recollect (one word, no hyphen) with re-collect (hyphenated).

  • Recollect = to remember
  • Re-collect = to collect something again (for example, "They had to re-collect the scattered papers.")

The hyphen makes all the difference. In almost all everyday usage, when you see "recollect" written as a single word without a hyphen, it means to remember.

Recollect means to deliberately and consciously bring a memory back to mind — to search your memory and retrieve something from the past. It emphasizes the active, often effortful nature of the act of remembering. It is slightly more formal and reflective in tone than everyday "remember," and it is especially at home when the memory is distant, uncertain, or requires some careful thought to retrieve.
